The proposed system, called geologic seawater air conditioning (GeoSWAC), leverages inland wells hydrologically connected to deep, cold seawater through permeable subsurface formations, eliminating a refrigeration cycle to produce cooling. While conventional SWAC systems require long offshore pipelines in coastal environments, GeoSWAC configuration reduces infrastructure costs, minimizes environmental impacts, and improves resilience by reducing dependence on grid-supplied electricity. The SWAC systems simplify the cooling process by avoiding energy-intensive refrigeration cycles and using minimal moving parts and no refrigerants. Electricity consumption of 75%–90% can be reduced the SWAC systems compared to chiller-based cooling systems (TEC Inc 2009; Lilley et al. 2015). The system offers substantial operational cost savings and improved resilience during power outages, as the system can run on backup generators or batteries. While the SWAC system has been extensively developed and deployed worldwide (e.g., Sanjivy et al. 2023), the hydrogeologic behavior and techno-economic performance of GeoSWAC have not been systematically evaluated motivating the present study. To evaluate the economic value of GeoSWAC system, a case study was conducted at a coastal university campus in San Juan—the Universidad de Puerto Rico Río Piedras. Surface and subsurface characteristics were investigated through building energy modeling, a site visit, and extensive literature review. While in-depth modeling of the hydraulic connection between inland wells and deep, cold seawater in the GeoSWAC system remains for future study, economic metrics were estimated and compared with those of a water-cooled chiller system at the campus. Results demonstrated that GeoSWAC system has significantly lower levelized costs of cooling and operational costs, along with water conservation through the elimination of evaporative and blowdown losses from cooling tower operation. Key advantages of GeoSWAC systems can include access to a constant cold heat sink from deep seawater, minimal pumping requirements due to favorable hydraulic gradients, and increased resilience during grid failures in areas like Puerto Rico, the Caribbean, and coastal Florida. However, the system’s performance is contingent on local geologic conditions, particularly the hydraulic connection between inland wells and deep cold seawater through a permeable formation. Uncertainties in the deep geological condition and aquifer characteristics in the San Juan Metropolitan Area must be addressed through detailed geologic and hydrogeologic surveys and site-specific performance modeling. v This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
